title: The same task cost $0.012 on GLM and $0.23 on Opus
summary: The same task ran for $0.012 on GLM 5.3 Flash and $0.23 on Opus 5.5 on our public eval page. What the cost column shows, and where the cheap model misses.
body_markdown:
*A perfect score on our eval page costs 19× more than a 98.2. That trade is sometimes worth it, and you can only tell once it has a price.*


The same Search Console analysis task cost $0.012 to run on GLM 5.3 Flash and $0.23 on Opus 5.5. Both answers sit in full on[our model showcase](https://www.vybe.build/models/showcase) , next to the score each one earned: 98.2% against 100%. We build Vybe, so weigh our numbers accordingly. This post is about the cost column on that page and what it changed for us.


If you pick models for a living, price each point of score before you admire it. On the task above, the last 1.8 points cost 19× the money. Sometimes that trade is worth it. With the price on the page, you can make the call deliberately.


## What the eval page measures


The page runs 15 tasks taken from day-to-day work, across sales, marketing and recruiting, from easy to hard. Each task has its own checklist: the facts a good answer must include, the instructions it must follow and the mistakes it must avoid, like inventing a detail or changing a file it was only asked to read. Every run starts from a fresh agent with the same data and tools. A mix of deterministic checks and a separate AI judge reviews each item, a check passes only when it is clearly met, and the score is the share of checks passed, averaged over five runs. Cost is not part of the score. Prices and scores below were re-checked against the page on November 5, 2026.


## Pricing the same task three ways


The task with the widest spread is a marketing job: read a 90-day Search Console export, find the queries gaining and losing clicks, the pages with high impressions and low CTR, then propose fixes. All three models got the same export.


Model Effort Cost per run Time Score


GLM 5.3 Flash Max $0.012 2.2 min 98.2%


Opus 5.5 Medium $0.23 56s 100%


GPT-6 Astra Medium $0.50 70s 100%


GLM ran at Max effort here while Opus and Astra ran at Medium. The page prints the configuration for every run, and even at full effort GLM's bill came to $0.012. Opus paid $0.23 for the same job, about 19× more. Astra's $0.50 makes it about 42× the GLM price ($0.50 against $0.012), and the extra spend bought nothing Opus hadn't already delivered at $0.23.


A 98.2% means GLM missed checks. The page publishes the full answer, so you can go read exactly which ones. On a checklist, a miss is a concrete thing: an invented detail, or a file edited that should only have been read. Whether those misses matter depends on the task, and the page leaves that judgment to you.


## Where the cheap model loses worst


Averaged over the 15 tasks, GLM scores 97.1% against 99.0% for Opus and 98.4% for GPT-6 Astra. The gap varies by team. Sales sits at 96.2% for GLM against 97.4% for Opus, a 1.2-point gap on work that costs $15 per 1,000 tasks on GLM and $251 on Opus. Recruiting is the outlier: 95.0% for GLM, 99.7% for Opus, 100% for Astra. A 4.7-point gap is a different animal from 1.2, and recruiting is the one team here where a missed check could reach a candidate. It is also the clearest case for paying premium rates.


## What the price gap turns into


On the page's calculator, 10,000 tasks a month cost $2,536 on Opus 5.5 and $183 on GLM, a difference of $2,354 every month, about $28,000 a year. The reverse reading is more useful: hold the bill at $2,536 and buy GLM tasks at the page's $0.018 per task. The same budget covers about 141,000 tasks ($2,536 divided by $0.018). We don't need 141,000 tasks a month, and we don't want a $28,000 bill either. What the headroom buys is routing freedom. The premium model gets the tasks where its two points pay. The cheap one gets everything else, and the bill stays small compared with the all-premium quote.


We keep a separate writeup for the rest of the bill, prompts and history included:[how we cut our AI agent bill](https://www.vybe.build/blog/how-to-cut-your-ai-agent-bill) .


## Shopping a benchmark page


The showcase is ours, so treat this list as the checklist we hold ourselves to. Four things make a cost column worth trusting. Prices come from each provider's public rates and cover every step the model takes along the way, final answer included. Every model gets the same task, data and tools, with the configuration printed next to each run, effort level included. Scores and costs are averages over five runs. And the failures stay visible: full answers on the page, checklist misses included, even when the cheap model is the one being sold. If an eval page hides one of those four, you have no way to check its numbers. Ask for them before you pick.


## What the scores still miss


Checklist grading has a ceiling. A run can pass every check and still read like a machine wrote it. The deterministic checks and the AI judge catch what can be checked, and the rest gets human review, which is a cost the cost column doesn't show. The question we haven't settled: how much of the two-point gap lives in the part no checklist reaches? It matters most on onboarding, because a first session is short, ambiguous and guidance-heavy, the kind of interaction where premium models do their best work. Onboarding is the one place we haven't ruled out paying premium rates.


We run our agents on GLM 5.3 Flash, 14× cheaper than Opus 5.5 by the page's math, and we publish the runs where it loses. The practice is simpler than the debate: publish the price and the misses, then decide task by task. If your platform publishes evals, check that the cost column and the failed checks are on the page. If they aren't, ask for them. And if you find a page that shows both and still says the premium model wins on your workload, believe it. We would.
